questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Note that plugging in $x=2$ gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ However, we can use L'Hopital's rule to find this limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{{x}^{2}+x-6}{{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{[{x}^{2}+x-6]^{′}}{[{x}^{2}-4]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{2x+1}{2x} \\  & =\frac{2(2)+1}{2(2)} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=-4$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{(x+4)^{3}}{3\sqrt[3]{x+5}-x-7} & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{{[(x+4)^{3}]}^{′}}{{[3(x+5)^{1/3}-x-7]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{3(x+4)^{2}}{(x+5)^{-2/3}-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{3(x+4)^{2}}{(x+5)^{-2/3}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{{[3(x+4)^{2}]}^{′}}{{[(x+5)^{-2/3}-1]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{6(x+4)}{-\frac{2}{3}(x+5)^{-5/3}} \\  & =-9{lim}_{x\to -4}(x+4)(x+5)^{5/3} \\  & =-9(-4+4)\,(-4+5)^{5/3} \\  & =-9\cdot 0\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}+8)=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\frac{1}{{x}^{6}})}{(\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}+8)} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}]}^{′}}{{[\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}+8]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(-\frac{6}{{x}^{7}})}{(-\frac{4}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{6{x}^{-7}}{4{x}^{-5}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{3}{2{x}^{2}} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying L'Hopital's rule yields

$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}+\sqrt{x}}{{x}^{2}-5\sqrt{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{[2x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}]}^{′}}{{[2x-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{x}}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{[2x+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-1/2}]}^{′}}{{[2x-\frac{5}{2}{x}^{-1/2}]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/2}}{2+\frac{5}{4}{x}^{-3/2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2-\frac{1}{4{x}^{3/2}}}{2+\frac{5}{4{x}^{3/2}}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac {\left[\sin^2 (2x)\right]'}{[x^2]'}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{2\cdot \sin (2x) \cdot\cos (2x)\cdot 2}{2x}\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}{2\cos (2x)} \cdot \lim_{x\to 0} \dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\cos(2\cdot 0)\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}
}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\dfrac{0}{0}.$ But that's okay, because we can just apply L'Hopital's rule again! We get

$$
\eqalign{
\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac{\sin^2 (2x)}{x^2} &= 2\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin (2x)}{x}\[5pt]
&=  2\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac {[\sin (2x)]'}{[x]'}\[5pt]
&=  2\lim_{x\to0}  \dfrac {2\cos (2x)}{1}\[5pt]
&= 4\cos(2\cdot 0)\
&=4.
}
$$

so we have the case $\dfrac{-\infty}{\infty}$.

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$

\lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)} &= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{[\ln\left(x^2\right)]'}{\left(\dfrac{2}{x^2}\right)'}\[5pt]

&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{x^{-2} \cdot 2x}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= \lim_{x\to 0}  \dfrac{2x^{-1}}{-4x^{-3} }\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2}  \lim_{x\to 0} {x^2}\[5pt]
&= -\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 0\[5pt]
&= 0.
}
$$
